body_html:
Every language has words that seem to capture a whole scene in a single breath. Spanish is full of them. These Spanish words with no English translation describe feelings, habits and relationships that English can only explain with a sentence: the conversation that lingers after a meal, the joy of wearing something new for the first time, the embarrassment you feel for someone else. Learning them is a lovely way to understand not just the language, but the life behind it.

Key takeaways
  • “Untranslatable” words can be explained, but not in a single English word.
  • Many of them reveal cultural values like family, food and time together.
  • They are easy to remember because they carry a story or feeling.
  • Use them in real sentences to make them part of your Spanish.
{{toc}}

What makes a word “untranslatable”?

Strictly speaking, any word can be translated with enough explanation. What we mean by Spanish words with no English translation is that English lacks a single equivalent word. These gaps are fascinating because they show what a culture finds worth naming. A language that has a word for lingering at the table after lunch clearly values that time.

Bilingual people often reach for these words even when speaking English, simply because nothing else fits. That kind of mixing is natural, as I explain in {{link:code-switching-english-spanish|code-switching between English and Spanish}}.

16 Spanish words with no English translation

WordMeaning
sobremesaThe relaxed conversation that lingers at the table after a meal, when nobody wants to leave.
estrenarTo use or wear something for the very first time: Hoy estreno zapatos.
madrugarTo get up very early, before or around dawn. A madrugador is an early riser.
friolero / frioleraA person who feels cold easily and always needs a sweater.
empalagosoSo sweet it becomes sickly; also used for someone overly affectionate.
consuegrosThe parents of your child’s spouse. English has no single word for this relationship.
tocayo / tocayaSomeone who shares your first name.
vergüenza ajenaThe embarrassment you feel on behalf of someone else.
antojoA sudden craving for a specific food, or a whim.
merendarTo have an afternoon snack (la merienda).
desvelarseTo lie awake, unable to sleep, or to stay up late on purpose.
aprovecharTo make the most of something; ¡Buen provecho! wishes someone a good meal.
querenciaA place where you feel safe and at home, where your strength comes from.
ojaláHopefully, if only; from an old Arabic phrase meaning “if God wills”.
puenteLiterally “bridge”: a long weekend created by taking a day off between a holiday and the weekend.
anteayerThe day before yesterday, in a single word.
{{image:2}}

Words about food and time together

Sobremesa

Perhaps the most famous example. After a meal, especially a long weekend lunch, families and friends stay at the table talking, laughing and drinking coffee. That unhurried time is la sobremesa. Nos quedamos de sobremesa hasta las seis. We stayed chatting at the table until six.

Merendar and antojo

La merienda is the afternoon snack, a cherished ritual for children and adults alike. An antojo is a sudden craving: Tengo antojo de chocolate.

Words about people and relationships

Consuegros

Your consuegros are the parents of your son-in-law or daughter-in-law. English needs a whole phrase; Spanish, with its strong focus on extended family, has one word.

Tocayo

Meet someone with your first name and you can greet them as ¡Hola, tocayo! It instantly creates a small bond.

Friolero

We all know a friolera: the person who brings a sweater to the beach. Its opposite, someone who is always warm, is a caluroso.

{{book:the-mind-lies}}

Words about feelings

Vergüenza ajena

Watching someone embarrass themselves and cringing on their behalf? That is vergüenza ajena, literally “someone else’s shame”. English sometimes borrows the German word for a related feeling, but Spanish has its own beautiful phrase.

Querencia

Originally used for the spot in the bullring where a bull feels safest, querencia came to mean the place where you feel most yourself, your home ground. It shares a root with querer, the verb behind te quiero, which I explore in {{link:te-quiero-vs-te-amo|te quiero vs te amo}}.

Ojalá

Ojalá expresses hope or a wish: Ojalá que llueva. I hope it rains. It comes from Arabic, a reminder of the centuries when Arabic was spoken in much of the Iberian Peninsula. Note that it is followed by the subjunctive.

{{image:3}}

Words about everyday life

  • Estrenar: the small thrill of using something new. ¿Estrenas vestido? Is that a new dress?
  • Madrugar: the proverb A quien madruga, Dios le ayuda means roughly “God helps those who get up early”.
  • Desvelarse: Anoche me desvelé pensando en el trabajo. I lay awake last night thinking about work.
  • Puente: a long weekend made by bridging a holiday and the weekend, especially common in Spain.

How to learn and use these words

  1. Learn them in a sentence. Save examples like Me encanta la sobremesa con mi familia, a habit I describe in {{link:sentence-mining-spanish|sentence mining}}.
  2. Connect them to your life. Are you a friolero or a madrugador? Describe yourself in Spanish.
  3. Use them with Spanish speakers. Native speakers are often delighted when a learner uses sobremesa or vergüenza ajena naturally.
  4. Look up regional variations. Some words are more common in Spain, others in Latin America. The Real Academia Española dictionary notes where words are used.

These words are a reminder that being bilingual means having more ways to name your experience. To see how that fits into the bigger picture, read my complete guide to {{link:bilingual-english-and-spanish|bilingual English and Spanish}}, and for more on why it matters, {{link:benefits-of-being-bilingual|the real benefits of being bilingual}}.

Final thoughts

Untranslatable words are small windows into how people live and what they treasure. Learn a few, use them with care and enjoy the moment someone smiles because you found exactly the right word. Next time a meal ends and nobody wants to leave, you will know what to call it.

faq.q: What is a Spanish word with no English translation?
faq.a: Sobremesa is a classic example: the relaxed conversation that continues at the table after a meal. English needs a whole sentence to express it.
It means feeling embarrassed on behalf of someone else, like cringing when a person you are watching makes an awkward mistake.

faq.q: Where does the word ojalá come from?
faq.a: Ojalá comes from an Arabic expression meaning roughly “if God wills”, a trace of the centuries when Arabic was spoken in much of Spain.
